A1.justification: Both PDFs are readable versions of the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices support comparison, including matching relocated ablations and MISTRAL results.

before.justification: V1 reports original routing and cascading evaluations on RouterBench, classification, and open-form reasoning tasks, plus runtime ablations and five-shot appendix results.

after.justification: V2 retains original empirical evaluations and adds SWE-Bench data analysis, math/code experiments, estimator sensitivity experiments, and runtime scaling results.

M1.justification: The core routing, supermodel selection, pruning, and hyperparameter optimization procedures remain intact. Appendix F.2 introduces MAX-DEPTH, an optional variant that restricts cascade routing to three computed models, constituting a limited inference-procedure change.

E1.justification: V2 adds SWE-Bench Verified software issue resolution and a combined Minerva Math Algebra/LiveCodeBench evaluation. These substantially extend the evaluated data and task coverage. The original RouterBench, classification, and open-form reasoning coverage remains, including MISTRAL results moved into the appendix.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain linear interpolation, routing, threshold cascading, and the authors' cascading strategy. The new runtime comparison adds MAX-DEPTH alongside standard cascade routing, SLOW, GREEDY, and NO-EXPECT. The added agent and QWEN pools are model configurations rather than new competing selection methods.

E3.justification: New experiments introduce 50/50 training/calibration partitions, SWE-Bench agent pools, four QWEN models, ground-truth post-hoc SWE quality feedback, and costs measured through execution time or tokens multiplied by model size. Runtime scaling uses 100 random inputs per model count. The original splits, shot settings, and three standard noise configurations are retained.

E4.justification: V2 adds a two-dimensional noise sweep examining the distinct effects of ex-ante and post-hoc estimation accuracy (Figure 2). Appendix F.2 adds scalability testing up to 80 models and examines depth restriction. The original eleven-model design ablation is retained in Appendix F.1 rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: V1 provides no comparable statistical intervals. V2 introduces sample-bootstrap intervals for AUC scores and paired AUC differences in Tables 4–6, together with significance-related table markings. This substantially changes uncertainty reporting; it does not establish additional model runs, and bootstrap resample counts and seeds are unspecified.

E6.justification: V2 adds SWE-Bench, Math+Code, noise-sweep, scaling, and benchmark-specific results. Existing entries also change: eleven-model low-noise cascade-routing AUC becomes 87.24 instead of 87.28, and MISTRAL open-form AUC becomes 58.73 instead of 58.69. Some new reporting is inconsistent: Table 5 gives a −0.64 five-shot difference where Table 10 implies +0.64.

T1.justification: Equation (1) replaces the joint expectation over queries and model indices with an explicit probability-weighted model sum inside the query expectation, aligning the main objective and budget expression with the existing Appendix A formulation. The theorems, assumptions, corollaries, and proofs in Appendices A–C otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction add a central contribution concerning when routing and cascading are useful, distinguishing ex-ante from post-hoc estimator requirements and explicitly rejecting the necessity of varying model sizes for cascading. The introduction also expands its headline empirical claims to the added evaluation settings. The original optimality and unification claims remain.

C2.justification: V2 substantially develops the interpretation of estimator accuracy, explains threshold cascading's failure with binary SWE-Bench feedback, and recommends depth restriction under suitable conditions. However, v1's explicit limitation concerning cascade routing's greater training-data and hyperparameter-fitting requirements is omitted. The appendix explanation of suboptimal five-shot cascading remains.

D1.justification: Appendix D adds substantial reproduction information: SWE-Bench log provenance and agent identifiers, exact QWEN models, LiveCodeBench version 5, evaluation-harness use, and benchmark-specific estimator features and cost calculations. Existing classification/open-form implementation details are retained or relocated. The declared code access remains unchanged.

R1.justification: V2 adds targeted discussion of confidence-token routing, routing during token generation, and multi-objective cascading, citing Chuang, Pichlmeier, and Zhang respectively. It also adds references supporting the new evaluations and challenges prior assumptions about model-size variation. The overall positioning around routing and cascading remains recognizable.

P1.justification: V2 substantially rewrites the abstract and introduction, adds method-section overviews, and reorganizes practical experiments around accurate versus poor quality estimation. Ablations move into the appendix, the standalone limitations and reproducibility sections disappear, and an impact statement is added. These constitute substantial narrative and structural revisions.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column to a two-column layout. The original quality-cost Figure 2 is replaced by noise heatmaps, a runtime scaling figure is added, and Table 2 is restructured. New confidence and benchmark-specific tables substantially expand the displays, while existing ablation and MISTRAL tables are relocated.

improvement.justification: V1 showed limited practical gains and examined runtime only at eleven models. V2's contrasting estimator regimes, noise sweeps, and scaling analysis substantially clarify applicability and computational limits, while bootstrap reporting makes statistical support more assessable. SWE-Bench still assumes ground-truth post-hoc feedback. Removing the explicit training-data limitation and introducing reporting conflicts, notably Tables 5 versus 10, weaken particular claims, but these shortcomings do not outweigh the substantial gains in explanatory and empirical support.
